title: Logic and evidence; correlation vs causation
blurb: Tell inductive from deductive reasoning, explain why correlation is not causation, and judge which conclusions the evidence really supports.
question: A headline reads 'Daily coffee drinkers live longer', based on a survey of 20,000 adults. Does this show that coffee causes longer life, what else could explain the link, and what kind of study would be needed to test it?

teach.body: Formally, a scientific explanation is based on empirical evidence (observation and measurement), is testable and falsifiable, can be reproduced by others and stays open to revision when new evidence appears. In plain English: it rests on things you can see or measure, it could be shown wrong, other people can check it, and it changes if the facts change. Opinions, appeals to authority and one-off stories do not meet this bar.

teach.h: Four marks of a scientific claim

items.label: falsifiable: some result could show it wrong
others can repeat it and get the same result

teach.caption: Peer review checks methods and conclusions before a study is published.

rows.label: Example
values: Every swan seen is white: all swans are
Mammals have hair; a whale is one: it has hair

rows.label: Certainty
values: Certain IF the premises are true

teach.caption: Memory hook: INduction goes INto the big picture from small cases; DEduction DEscends from the big rule to one case.

teach.body: A correlation means two variables change together. It does not show that one causes the other. Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer, but hot weather drives both. Only a controlled experiment, where the researcher changes one variable and holds the rest constant, can establish cause and effect. Observational and survey data can reveal a link worth testing, nothing more.

teach.h: A and B rise together: four possible reasons
teach.caption: Before accepting 'A causes B', rule out the other three branches.

teach.body: Elena, a pre-nursing student, sees 'Daily coffee drinkers live longer'. The study surveyed 20,000 adults: observational, so it shows an association only. A third variable could drive both: people with more income or free time may drink more coffee and also get better health care. To test causation, researchers would need a controlled experiment with random assignment, which may be impractical over a lifetime. Elena's sound conclusion: coffee drinking is linked to longer life in this population.

teach.h: Support, refute and stay inside the data
teach.body: Evidence that agrees with a hypothesis supports it; it never proves it. But one well-replicated contradicting result can refute it. A sound conclusion stays within the data: the same population, the same conditions and the range actually tested. Do not extrapolate far beyond the data, and acknowledge sample size and error.

rows.label: In 40 adults aged 20-30, the drug lowered blood pressure.
The drug lowers blood pressure in everyone.
Ten times the tested dose will work even better.
The study proves the drug works.

head: Ask
Red flag
rows: Is it data or a story?
teach.caption: Popularity and authority are not evidence. A claim stands on its data.

teach.text: Watch for: inductive and deductive swapped; causation concluded from a correlation or a survey; 'the experiment proved the hypothesis'; a result from one group generalized to everyone; and a claim accepted because an authority or many people believe it.

items: Scientific claims are empirical, testable (falsifiable), reproducible and revisable.
Inductive: specific to general (probable). Deductive: general to specific (certain if premises are true).
Correlation is not causation: consider a third variable, reverse causation or coincidence.
Only a controlled experiment can establish cause and effect.
Data support or refute; one well-replicated contradiction can refute a hypothesis.
Conclusions stay within the population, conditions and range tested.

summary: You can now identify inductive and deductive reasoning, explain a correlation through a third variable, reverse causation or coincidence, and recognize that only a controlled experiment shows cause and effect. You can also judge a claim's evidence and keep a conclusion within what the data show.

A.q: A nurse notices that none of the last 30 patients given a new adhesive bandage developed skin irritation, and concludes that the bandage does not irritate skin. What kind of reasoning is this?
options: Deductive: specific cases to a general rule
Deductive: a general rule to a specific case
Inductive: specific cases to a general rule
Inductive: a general rule to a specific case
A.why: Moving from many specific observations (30 patients) to a general conclusion is inductive reasoning. The conclusion is probable, and one irritated patient could overturn it.

whyNot.0: The direction is right, but specific-to-general reasoning is called inductive, not deductive.
whyNot.1: Deductive reasoning goes from a general premise to a specific case; here the nurse builds a general rule.
whyNot.3: Inductive is the right name, but the direction is reversed: the nurse goes from cases to a rule.

A.q: Cities with more hospitals also report more deaths each year. What is the MOST likely explanation?
options: Population size drives both numbers
Hospitals cause more deaths to occur
More deaths lead to more hospitals
The link is a statistical coincidence
A.why: Bigger cities have more people, so they have both more hospitals and more deaths: population is a third (confounding) variable.

whyNot.1: This treats a correlation as causation without ruling out a third variable.
whyNot.2: Reverse causation is possible in principle, but city size explains both far more simply.
whyNot.3: A strong, consistent link across many cities is unlikely to be chance when an obvious third variable exists.

A.q: Which is the STRONGEST reason to accept a scientific claim?
options: A well-known celebrity doctor endorses it
Most people in a national poll believe it
A patient described dramatic results
Independent teams have replicated it
A.why: Reproducibility is a mark of scientific evidence: independent replication shows the result is not a fluke or the product of one team's bias.

whyNot.0: An endorsement is an appeal to authority, not evidence.
whyNot.1: Popularity is not evidence; many people can believe something false.
whyNot.2: A single testimonial is anecdotal and has no control or sample.

B.q: A hypothesis states that a disinfectant kills all bacteria on a surface. Twenty trials support it. Then a well-replicated trial finds surviving bacteria. What should be concluded?
options: The hypothesis stands, since 20 trials agree
The hypothesis is refuted by the new result
The hypothesis is proven true by the majority
The new trial should be dropped as an outlier
B.why: Supporting evidence never proves a hypothesis, but one well-replicated contradicting result can refute it.

whyNot.0: Agreement in earlier trials does not outweigh a replicated counterexample to an 'all' claim.
whyNot.2: Scientific hypotheses are not decided by a majority of results; they are never proven.
whyNot.3: A replicated result is not an outlier; discarding it would ignore evidence.

B.q: 'All arteries carry blood away from the heart. The aorta is an artery. Therefore, the aorta carries blood away from the heart.' Which statement about this reasoning is CORRECT?
options: Deductive; certain if the premises are true
Inductive; probable but open to a counterexample
Deductive; it builds a general rule from cases
Inductive; it moves from one case to a rule
B.why: The argument applies a general premise to a specific case, which is deductive. If the premises are true, the conclusion must be true.

whyNot.1: Inductive conclusions are probable, but this argument goes from general to specific, so it is deductive.
whyNot.2: Deductive is the right name, but it applies a rule to a case; it does not build a rule from cases.
whyNot.3: The argument starts from a general rule, not from one case.

B.q: A study of 500 women aged 20-35 finds that a vitamin supplement reduced fatigue compared with a placebo. Which conclusion is justified?
options: It reduces fatigue in adults of every age and sex
A triple dose would reduce fatigue even more
It reduced fatigue in women like those studied
It proves low vitamins are a cause of fatigue
B.why: A sound conclusion stays within the population and conditions tested: women aged 20-35 at the dose studied.

whyNot.0: This generalizes beyond the population tested (men, children and older adults were not studied).
whyNot.1: This extrapolates beyond the dose range tested.
whyNot.3: Data support conclusions; they do not 'prove' them, and the study tested the supplement, not the cause of fatigue.

C.q: A survey of 8,000 adults finds that those who drink green tea daily have lower blood pressure than those who do not. Which conclusion is BEST supported?
options: Drinking green tea lowers blood pressure in adults
Lower blood pressure makes people drink green tea
The survey proves tea prevents high blood pressure
Green tea use is linked to lower blood pressure
C.why: A survey is observational. It can show an association, but not cause and effect.

whyNot.0: Concluding causation from a correlation; tea drinkers may differ in diet, exercise or income.
whyNot.1: This proposes reverse causation, which the survey cannot show either.
whyNot.2: No study 'proves' a claim, and an observational survey cannot establish prevention.

C.q: Among children aged 5 to 12, those with larger shoe sizes score higher on reading tests. Which explanation is MOST likely?
options: Larger feet giving children more self-confidence
Age, which raises both shoe size and reading
Reading practice causing faster foot growth
Random chance in an unusually small sample
C.why: Older children have bigger feet AND read better. Age is a third (confounding) variable that drives both.

whyNot.0: This treats the correlation as causation without checking for a third variable.
whyNot.2: This proposes reverse causation with no supporting evidence, when age explains both.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests a small sample, and a clear confounding variable is available.

C.q: A company that sells a memory supplement funds a study in which 12 of its customers report feeling sharper after taking it. There is no comparison group. Which change would do MOST to show whether the supplement CAUSES better memory?
options: Survey 1,200 of its customers instead of 12
Have a well-known doctor endorse the results
Randomly assign supplement or placebo
Publish the findings in a press release
C.why: Cause and effect needs a controlled experiment: random assignment to the supplement or a placebo gives a comparison group and removes self-selection.

whyNot.0: A larger sample improves reliability, but without a control group it still cannot show causation.
whyNot.1: An endorsement is an appeal to authority, not evidence.
whyNot.3: Publicizing results does nothing to fix the missing control group or the conflict of interest.

reteach.title: Roosters and the sunrise
reteach.question: A rooster crows every morning just before the sun rises. Does the rooster make the sun come up? How does this everyday example explain correlation and causation?

blocks.h: Always together is not the same as cause
blocks.body: The crowing and the sunrise happen together every single day: a perfect correlation. Yet silencing the rooster would not stop the sunrise. If anything, the coming dawn prompts the crowing, so assuming 'crowing causes sunrise' gets the direction backward. The only way to know what causes what is to change one thing on purpose and watch what happens: that is a controlled experiment.

steps.label: Change one thing
steps.sub: Keep the rooster quiet one morning

steps.label: Conclude
steps.sub: Yes: crowing does not cause sunrise

blocks.text: However strong or consistent a correlation is, it cannot by itself tell you which variable causes which, or whether a third variable drives both.

explain.body: A scientific claim is based on empirical evidence, is testable and falsifiable, can be reproduced by others, and is revised when new evidence appears.

test.q: Which claim could be investigated scientifically?
options: Drinking 2 L of water daily lowers resting pulse
Classical music is more beautiful than jazz
Undetectable spirits guide each patient's recovery
People ought to exercise more than they do now
test.why: Water intake and resting pulse can both be measured, and a test could show the claim is false: it is testable and falsifiable.

whyNot.1: Beauty is a matter of opinion and cannot be measured objectively.
whyNot.2: Something undetectable cannot be observed or measured, so the claim cannot be tested.
whyNot.3: This is a value judgment about what people should do, not a testable prediction.

explain.body: Inductive reasoning goes from specific observations to a general conclusion (probable). Deductive reasoning goes from a general premise to a specific conclusion (certain if the premises are true).

options: a general premise to a specific conclusion
a hypothesis straight to a scientific law
a single anecdote to a certain conclusion
specific cases to a general conclusion
test.why: Induction builds a general conclusion from specific observations.

whyNot.1: Hypotheses do not turn into laws, and this is not a type of reasoning.
whyNot.2: Inductive conclusions are probable, never certain, and one anecdote is weak evidence.

explain.body: When two variables move together, the cause may be a third variable, the direction may be reversed, or it may be coincidence. Only a controlled experiment establishes causation.

test.q: Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. Why does this NOT show that ice cream causes drowning?
options: The data show drowning causes ice cream sales
Hot weather is a third variable driving both
The two variables are not measured in numbers
Summer data cannot be graphed on a scatterplot
test.why: Hot weather increases both swimming and ice-cream buying, so it is a confounding third variable.

whyNot.0: This is reverse causation, which the data do not show either.
whyNot.2: Both are counts, which are numerical (quantitative) data.
whyNot.3: Two numeric variables can be shown on a scatterplot; graphing is not the issue.

explain.body: Agreeing evidence supports a hypothesis but never proves it; one well-replicated contradicting result can refute it. Conclusions must stay within the population, conditions and range tested.

test.q: A well-designed study supports a researcher's hypothesis. Which statement is CORRECT?
options: The hypothesis is now proven and can no longer change
A later well-replicated result could refute it
The hypothesis has now become a scientific theory
Other researchers do not need to replicate it
test.why: Supporting evidence never proves a hypothesis; future well-replicated evidence could still contradict it.

whyNot.0: Scientific conclusions are always open to revision.
whyNot.2: A theory rests on many lines of evidence, not one supporting study.
whyNot.3: Replication by others is what makes a result reliable and scientific.
